ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. text:
After harvest, kernels need to be separated from the cob (shelling/threshing). This source describes a range of methods by scale:

- Hand shelling (twisting kernels off the cob by hand) is slow and labour-intensive.
- A simple hand-crank sheller can process roughly 8-15 kg/hour, which the source describes as suitable for individual household-scale needs; quality can be inconsistent (some kernel breakage and loss from irregular cranking, and debris/trash in the cobs can affect the machine).
- Motorised shellers, powered by an engine and used with a rotating drum/disc mechanism, can process roughly 300-900 kg/hour depending on the model and engine size -- much better suited to a farmer group or larger commercial operation than to an individual smallholder, given the equipment cost. In corn-growing areas such as Kampong Cham, motorised shellers sized for smallholder budgets are reported to be in common use.
